key_concept: For near-normal viewing across a single plane surface, apparent depth $= \text{real depth} \times \dfrac{n_{\text{observer}}}{n_{\text{object}}}$.
steps: The object $O$ is at the centre of the 5 cm slab $Q$. Its real distance from each face is $\dfrac{5}{2} = 2.5$ cm.
Viewing from $P$ means one refraction at the $Q$–$P$ face: $h_1 = 2.5 \times \dfrac{n_P}{n_Q} = 2.5 \times \dfrac{1}{1.25} = 2$ cm. The image appears closer, since light goes into a rarer medium.
Viewing from $R$ means one refraction at the $Q$–$R$ face: $h_2 = 2.5 \times \dfrac{n_R}{n_Q} = 2.5 \times \dfrac{1.5}{1.25} = 3$ cm. The image appears farther, since light goes into a denser medium.
why_not_others: Option (1) comes from using real/n for both sides, which ignores that viewing from the denser medium $R$ increases the apparent depth. Option (3) or (4) comes from using the full 5 cm thickness instead of 2.5 cm, or from comparing with the real depth.
common_trap: Students often apply the formula $\text{apparent} = \text{real}/n$ blindly from both sides. Doing so gives a smaller depth even when viewing from the denser medium $R$, where the depth should actually look larger.
time_saving_tip: Use $h_1 - h_2 = d\,\dfrac{n_P - n_R}{n_Q}$ directly: $|2.5 \times (1 - 1.5)/1.25| = 1$ cm.
